Part `05-ll-and-gonna.mp3` is new — the short *'ll* and the weak *going to*. ### 1.1 Before listening (2 minutes, Arabic is fine here) 1. What are you going to do this evening, and what will you do if the power goes off? 2. Who decides the order of jobs when you work with other people? 3. What is the first thing you charge when the electricity comes on? ### 1.4 Now read the passage ### Passage: *A Plan for Tuesday* (504 words) There are four of them, and between them they have one inverter, one battery, two laptops and a list. The list is on the back of a door in a room at the college, and every Sunday evening they write next week's plan on it. The plan is not about the work. The plan is about the power. Everything else on the list follows from that. **[A]** The electricity in their part of the city comes in two blocks, and the schedule changes every month. This month it is on from six in the morning until nine, and again from seven at night until eleven. Seven hours. Dalia, who keeps the list, says the first thing you learn is that seven hours is enough, if you decide what each hour is for before it starts. So the list has two columns. On the left is what they are going to do while the power is on: plug in both laptops, charge the battery, download the week's lecture videos, and send the group project up to the cloud. On the right is what they will do when it goes off: read, write, plan, and argue about the design. Every line has a name beside it, so nobody is waiting for somebody else to begin. **[B]** Yousef is in charge of the downloads. "I am going to start the big files at six," he said on Sunday, "and I'll leave the small ones until the end. If the bandwidth is bad, we will still have the lectures." He has learned not to queue everything at once. Last month he put eleven files in the queue at six o'clock and had four of them by nine. Nour is going to finish the database work before Thursday, because the deadline is Thursday night and she is going to submit it on time this week. Hani is going to rebuild the spare laptop, the one with the broken socket, and he says it will be ready by Wednesday. Nobody believes him. He says that every week. **[C]** There are rules on the list as well, and all of them are about priority. The battery is for the router first and the laptops second. Nothing that can be done on paper is done on a screen while the power is on. And whatever else happens, the project goes to the cloud before eleven, because a file that exists in one place does not really exist. **[D]** Dalia will not say that the plan always works. Last Tuesday the generator in the building below them failed at half past seven, and the two blocks became one. They lost three hours. But they had sent the project up at seven, so they lost three hours of work and nothing else, which is the whole reason for the rule. On Sunday she will write the next list, and it will look much like this one. "We are not going to get more hours," she says. "So we are going to get better at the hours we have." ### 1.5 Read aloud Read the passage aloud **once** and record it. Watch the two short forms as you read: say *I'll* and /ˈɡənə/, not *I will* and *going to*.

segments.say: Lesson six. A Plan for Tuesday. Listening practice.

You will hear about four students who plan their week around the hours of electricity. Listen for what they are going to do while the power is on, and what they will do when it goes off. You will hear it two times. Do not read the text. Listen only.

There are four of them, and between them they have one inverter, one battery, two laptops and a list. The list is on the back of a door in a room at the college, and every Sunday evening they write next week's plan on it. The plan is not about the work. The plan is about the power. Everything else on the list follows from that.

The electricity in their part of the city comes in two blocks, and the schedule changes every month. This month it is on from six in the morning until nine, and again from seven at night until eleven. Seven hours. Dalia, who keeps the list, says the first thing you learn is that seven hours is enough, if you decide what each hour is for before it starts.

So the list has two columns. On the left is what they are going to do while the power is on: plug in both laptops, charge the battery, download the week's lecture videos, and send the group project up to the cloud. On the right is what they will do when it goes off: read, write, plan, and argue about the design. Every line has a name beside it, so nobody is waiting for somebody else to begin.

Yousef is in charge of the downloads. "I am going to start the big files at six," he said on Sunday, "and I'll leave the small ones until the end. If the bandwidth is bad, we will still have the lectures." He has learned not to queue everything at once. Last month he put eleven files in the queue at six o'clock and had four of them by nine.

Nour is going to finish the database work before Thursday, because the deadline is Thursday night and she is going to submit it on time this week. Hani is going to rebuild the spare laptop, the one with the broken socket, and he says it will be ready by Wednesday. Nobody believes him. He says that every week.

There are rules on the list as well, and all of them are about priority. The battery is for the router first and the laptops second. Nothing that can be done on paper is done on a screen while the power is on. And whatever else happens, the project goes to the cloud before eleven, because a file that exists in one place does not really exist.

Dalia will not say that the plan always works. Last Tuesday the generator in the building below them failed at half past seven, and the two blocks became one. They lost three hours. But they had sent the project up at seven, so they lost three hours of work and nothing else, which is the whole reason for the rule.

On Sunday she will write the next list, and it will look much like this one. "We are not going to get more hours," she says. "So we are going to get better at the hours we have."

### 2.1 Key words

| # | Word | Type | Simple meaning | Arabic | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | inverter | noun | a machine that changes battery power into normal house power | عاكس كهربائي | Between them they have one **inverter** and one battery. |
| 2 | generator | noun | a machine that makes electricity from fuel | مولّد كهرباء | The **generator** in the building below them failed. |
| 3 | socket | noun | the hole in the wall that a machine takes power from | مقبس كهرباء | The spare laptop is the one with the broken **socket**. |
| 4 | plug in | verb | to join a machine to a socket so that it takes power | يوصل بالكهرباء | They **plug in** both laptops while the power is on. |
| 5 | download | verb | to bring a file from the internet onto your own machine | يُنزِّل ملفاً | They **download** the week's lecture videos at six. |
| 6 | bandwidth | noun | how much data a connection can carry at one time | سعة النطاق | If the **bandwidth** is bad, we will still have the lectures. |
| 7 | schedule | noun | a plan that says what happens at what time | جدول زمني | The **schedule** changes every month. |
| 8 | deadline | noun | the last day or hour when work can be given in | الموعد النهائي | The **deadline** is Thursday night. |
| 9 | cloud | noun | storage on the internet, instead of on your own machine | التخزين السحابي | The project goes to the **cloud** before eleven. |
| 10 | laptop | noun | a computer you can carry and close | حاسوب محمول | The battery is for the router first and the **laptops** second. |
| 11 | submit | verb | to send work in officially, for marking or for a decision | يُسلِّم | She is going to **submit** it on time this week. |
| 12 | spare | adjective | kept ready in case it is needed | احتياطي | Hani is going to rebuild the **spare** laptop. |
| 13 | priority | noun | the thing that must be done before anything else | أولوية | All of the rules are about **priority**. |
| 14 | queue | noun | a line of people or jobs waiting, one after another | طابور | He put eleven files in the **queue** at six o'clock. |

### 2.2 Synonyms and opposites

| Word | Synonym | Opposite |
|---|---|---|
| spare | extra, kept back | in use |
| priority | what comes first | what can wait |
| submit | hand in, send in | keep back |
| download | bring down | upload |
| deadline | the last moment | no fixed date |
| plug in | connect | unplug |
| queue | line, waiting list | straight through |
| on purpose | deliberately | by accident |

### 2.3 Expressions to learn

| Expression | What it really means |
|---|---|
| **in charge of** | responsible for; it is his job |
| **at once** | all at the same time |
| **on time** | not late |
| **whatever else happens** | even if everything else goes wrong |
| **get better at** | improve at doing something |
| **half past seven** | seven thirty |
| **nobody believes him** | everyone doubts what he says |

### 2.4 Vocabulary practice

**A. Write the opposite:**

4. plug in → \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

**B. Which word is different? Say why:**

1. inverter — generator — battery — deadline
2. download — submit — queue — spare
3. schedule — deadline — priority — socket

**C. Say it in your own words:**

1. What is bandwidth, and when do you notice it?
2. What does *priority* mean? Give an example from your own week.

parts.title: Grammar — the future with will and going to
parts.markdown:
### Come back to: the present perfect

Lesson 4 taught the shape, and *for*, *since*, *never*, *already* and *yet*.
Two lines to remind you:

| I / you / we / they | **have** finished |
|---|---|
| he / she / it | **has** finished |

**New this time: the present perfect and a finished time do not mix.**

The present perfect reaches from the past up to now, so it cannot sit beside a
time that is closed and gone:

- *She **has submitted** the project.* ✓ — no time given, and now is what matters
- *She **submitted** it on Thursday.* ✓ — Thursday is finished, so past simple
- *She has submitted it on Thursday.* ✗ — the two cannot be in one sentence

So **an exact date pushes you into the past simple**, however recent it is:

| With a finished time → past simple | With *for* or *since* → present perfect |
|---|---|
| They **lost** three hours last Tuesday. | They **have lost** three hours this week. |
| He **queued** eleven files at six o'clock. | He **has queued** files since six. |
| The generator **failed** at half past seven. | The generator **has failed** twice this month. |

*Last Tuesday*, *at six o'clock*, *yesterday*, *in 2023* — all finished, all
past simple. *This week*, *today*, *this month* are not finished yet, so the
present perfect is still at home in them.

**Quick practice.** Present perfect, or past simple?

1. The generator \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (fail) last Tuesday.
2. They \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (not lose) a single file this month.
3. He \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (put) eleven files in the queue at six o'clock.
4. Dalia \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (keep) the list since the first week.

---

Now the other direction. English has two ordinary ways to talk about the future,
and they are not the same: **going to** looks at a decision that has already
been made, and **will** looks at the moment of speaking.

### 3.1 How we make them

| | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *going to* | **am / is / are** + **going to** + verb | She **is going to submit** it on Thursday. |
| *will* | **will** + verb (no *to*, no *-s*) | It **will be** ready by Wednesday. |

*Will* is the same for everybody: *I will*, *she will*, *they will*. The short
form is **'ll** — *I'll*, *she'll*, *we'll* — and in speech that is almost all
you hear. Part 05 is about exactly that.

### 3.2 *Going to*: the plan that already exists

Use **going to** when the decision was taken **before** you opened your mouth.

- *I **am going to start** the big files at six.* — he decided on Sunday
- *Nour **is going to finish** the database work before Thursday.* — it is on the list
- *We **are not going to get** more hours.* — a fact she has already faced

It is also the future you can **see coming**, because the evidence is in front
of you:

- *Look at the battery — it **is going to die** in ten minutes.*
- *The sky is black. It **is going to rain**.*

### 3.3 *Will*: the moment of speaking

Use **will** for a decision, an offer, a promise or an opinion made **now**:

| Use | Example |
|---|---|
| Deciding as you speak | *The bandwidth is bad — I**'ll** download the small ones instead.* |
| Offering | *I**'ll** carry the battery for you.* |
| Promising | *It **will** be ready by Wednesday.* |
| Predicting, or giving an opinion | *I think the power **will** come back at seven.* |
| Refusing (negative) | *The old laptop **won't** start on battery.* |

Two of those matter most for her: **will** is what you use when you have just
this second decided, and **will** is what you use for what you *think* is going
to happen, with *I think*, *I am sure*, *probably*, *maybe*.

### 3.4 *Will* or *going to*?

| *Going to* — decided already | *Will* — decided now, or only an opinion |
|---|---|
| We **are going to** plug in both laptops at six. | If the bandwidth is bad, we **will** take the lectures first. |
| She **is going to** submit it on time this week. | I think she **will** finish before Thursday. |
| They **are going to** get better at the hours they have. | Dalia **will not** say that the plan always works. |

A short way to hold it: **the list is *going to*; the conversation is *will*.**
Anything written on the door was decided on Sunday. Anything said in the room at
six o'clock, while the power comes on and something has gone wrong, is *will*.

### 3.5 Negative and question

| | *going to* | *will* |
|---|---|---|
| Negative | She **is not going to** ask again. | It **will not** (**won't**) start. |
| Question | **Are** you **going to** queue them all? | **Will** it be ready by Wednesday? |
| Short answer | *Yes, I am. / No, I am not.* | *Yes, it will. / No, it won't.* |

### 3.6 Grammar practice

**A. *Going to* or *will*? Say why:**

1. Look at that battery. It \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (die) in ten minutes.
2. The bandwidth is bad tonight — I \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (take) the small files first.
3. It is on the list: we \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (plug in) both laptops at six.
4. I think the power \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (come back) at seven.
5. She \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (submit) it on Thursday. It has been planned for a week.

**B. Put the verb in the correct future form:**

1. Hani \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (rebuild) the spare laptop this week.
2. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ you \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (download) the lectures tonight?
3. They \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (not get) more hours of electricity.
4. The project \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (go) to the cloud before eleven.
5. I am sure the deadline \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (not move).

**C. Present perfect, or past simple?**

1. The generator \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (fail) at half past seven.
2. We \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (not miss) a deadline this month.
3. He \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (queue) eleven files last month.
4. Dalia \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (write) the list every Sunday since October.

parts.title: The short 'll and the weak going to
parts.markdown: ### 3.7 The short *'ll*, and the weak *going to* (listen to `05-ll-and-gonna.mp3`) The whole future tense can disappear into one sound. If you cannot hear it, you will think somebody is talking about now. **1. *will* becomes *'ll*, and *'ll* is one consonant.** | Written in full | What you hear | Not this | |---|---|---| | I will take it. | /aɪl ˈteɪk ɪt/ | /aɪ wɪl ˈteɪk ɪt/ | | It will be ready. | /ɪtl̩ bi ˈredi/ | /ɪt wɪl bi ˈredi/ | | We will still have them. | /wil stɪl ˈhæv ðəm/ | /wiː wɪl .../ | | She will finish it. | /ʃil ˈfɪnɪʃ ɪt/ | /ʃiː wɪl .../ | The full /wɪl/ comes back in three places only: at the end of a sentence (*Yes, it **will***), in the negative (***won't*** /wəʊnt/), and when the speaker is insisting. **2. *going to* becomes /ˈɡənə/.** Before another verb, *going to* loses almost everything. This is normal speech, not slang, and every speaker does it: | Written | What you actually hear | |---|---| | I am going to start at six. | /aɪm ˈɡənə ˈstɑːt ət sɪks/ | | She is going to submit it. | /ʃiz ˈɡənə səbˈmɪt ɪt/ | | We are going to get better. | /wə ˈɡənə ɡet ˈbetə/ | | They are not going to wait. | /ðeə nɒt ˈɡənə ˈweɪt/ | **Write *going to*. Say /ˈɡənə/.** The written form never changes; only the sound does. **3. One warning.** *going to* keeps its full sound when *going* is a real verb of movement: *I am **going to** the college* /ˈɡəʊɪŋ tuː/ — she is going somewhere, not planning something. In the audio you hear each line twice, and then a test: say whether what you hear is **will** or **going to**.

segments.say: Pronunciation. The short L L, and the weak going to.
The whole future tense can disappear into one sound. Listen to each line twice, then repeat it.
The full word will comes back at the end of a sentence, and in the negative. Listen.
Now going to. Before another verb it becomes gonna. This is normal speech, not slang. Write going to. Say gonna.
I'm going to start at six.
I'm going to start at six.
One warning. When going is a real verb of movement, it keeps its full sound. Listen to the difference.
I'm going to finish the work.
Now the test. You will hear a sentence. Say whether it uses will, or going to. Then you will hear the answer.
We're going to plug in both laptops.
She's going to submit it on Thursday.
I'm going to start the big files at six.
This is the end of the pronunciation practice.

parts.title: Comprehension — a full TOEFL set of ten
parts.markdown:
### Part A — Multiple choice

> This is a full set of ten, the size of a real TOEFL reading set.

**1. (Factual)** How many hours of electricity does their area get this month?

- A. Four.
- B. Seven.
- C. Eleven.
- D. Twenty-four.

**2. (Factual)** What is Yousef in charge of?

- A. The battery.
- B. The list.
- C. The downloads.
- D. The spare laptop.

**3. (Negative factual)** According to the passage, all of the following are on the left-hand column of the list EXCEPT

- A. plugging in both laptops.
- B. charging the battery.
- C. downloading the lecture videos.
- D. arguing about the design.

**4. (Vocabulary in context)** The word "priority" in the passage is closest in meaning to

- A. what comes first.
- B. what costs least.
- C. what is easiest.
- D. what is written down.

**5. (Reference)** In the sentence, he says it will be ready by Wednesday, the word "it" refers to

- A. the list.
- B. the spare laptop.
- C. the database work.
- D. the project.

**6. (Inference)** It can be inferred from the passage that the group

- A. expects the electricity to improve soon.
- B. has given up planning its week.
- C. treats the power schedule as something to plan around, not to complain about.
- D. does most of its work on paper.

**7. (Sentence insertion)** Look at the four letters **[A] [B] [C] [D]** in the passage. Where would this sentence best fit?

> *A plan is only worth anything on the week it is tested.*


- A. At **[A]**
- B. At **[B]**
- C. At **[C]**
- D. At **[D]**

**8. (Purpose of a paragraph)** Why does the writer mention the eleven files Yousef queued last month?

- A. To show that the connection is always slow.
- B. To explain why he now starts the big files first.
- C. To criticise Yousef for being careless.
- D. To show how many lectures there are each week.

**9. (Purpose of the whole passage)** What is the writer's main purpose in the whole passage?

- A. To explain how an inverter works.
- B. To ask the reader to send equipment to the group.
- C. To show how four students plan a week of study around the hours of electricity they get.
- D. To compare studying at home with studying at college.

**10. (The writer's attitude)** Which word best describes the writer's attitude towards the group's plan?

- A. Amused.
- B. Anxious.
- C. Respectful.
- D. Uninterested.

### Part C — Fill in the blanks

Use these words. There are **two extra words** you will not need.

> *inverter · schedule · deadline · cloud · queue · spare · priority · bandwidth · generator*

1. The \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ changes every month, so the plan changes with it.

### 5.2 Writing — "My Plan for Next Week" (14–16 sentences)

**Model answer (copy the shape, change the words):**

> Next week is going to be busy, so I wrote the plan down on Friday. I am going to finish the report for my course before Wednesday, because the deadline is Wednesday night and I am not going to ask for more time again. The electricity in our street comes on at six in the morning and again at eight at night. While it is on I am going to charge the laptop, download the two lectures I have missed, and put the finished chapters in the cloud. When it goes off I will read and make notes on paper, which costs nothing. My first priority is the report; everything else can wait. I think the hardest part will be Tuesday, because I have the class and the deadline on the same day. If the connection is slow I'll download the small files first and leave the videos until the morning. My sister is going to use the spare account for her own work, so we will not fight over the password. I have not planned Thursday yet. I will decide on Wednesday night, when I know what is left. The plan will not survive the week exactly as it is written, but a week with a plan is a different week from a week without one.

**Checklist before you send it:**

- [ ] I used **going to** at least **four** times, for decisions already made.
- [ ] I used **will** or **'ll** at least **four** times, for opinions and for decisions made in the moment.
- [ ] I used the past simple, not the present perfect, with a finished time.
- [ ] I used at least **5 new words** from Session 2.
- [ ] I used at least **2 words** from Lesson 4 or Lesson 5.
- [ ] My text has 14–16 sentences.

parts.title: Answer key and teacher notes
parts.markdown:
**Listening:** L1 — four students; they share one inverter, one battery, two laptops and a list · L2 — six to nine in the morning, and seven to eleven at night · L3 — he starts the big downloads · L4 — the generator in the building below failed at half past seven, and they lost three hours

**Part A (MCQ):** 1-B · 2-C · 3-D · 4-A · 5-B · 6-C · 7-D · 8-B · 9-C · 10-C

*Why 7 is **[D]***: the sentence is about a plan being tested, and only the paragraph after **[D]** tests one — the Tuesday the generator failed. The paragraph after **[A]** is the schedule, after **[B]** is one person's method, after **[C]** is the rules. None of those is a test of anything.

*Why 8 is **B***: the eleven files are there to explain what Yousef learned from them, and the next sentence is the lesson — he starts the big ones first now. The paragraph is not a complaint about the connection and not a criticism of him.

*Why 9 is **C***: the passage explains no machine, asks for nothing and compares nothing. It follows one week's list from Sunday to Sunday.

*Why 10 is **C, respectful***: as in Lesson 5, watch what is **chosen to be reported** rather than what is said about it. The writer gives the rules without comment, lets Dalia have the last word, and records the one week the plan failed — including the detail that the rule saved the work. There is no *brave* and no *sadly*. The respect is in the care taken over the detail.

**Part B (True/False):**

1. F — It is a plan for the power: what to do while it is on, and what to do when it is off.
2. T
3. F — He starts the big files at six and leaves the small ones until the end.
4. T
5. F — The router comes first and the laptops second.
6. F — They had sent it to the cloud at seven, so they lost only the time.

**Part C (Fill in the blanks):** 1. schedule · 2. inverter · 3. queue · 4. deadline · 5. cloud · 6. spare · 7. priority
*(Extra words: bandwidth, generator)*

**2.4 A (Opposites):** 1. in use · 2. upload · 3. keep back · 4. unplug · 5. what can wait

**2.4 B (Odd one out):** 1. deadline (the others make or hold electricity) · 2. spare (the others are things you do) · 3. socket (the others are about time or order)

**Come back to (present perfect or past simple):** 1. failed · 2. have not lost · 3. put · 4. has kept

**3.6 A (*going to* or *will*, and why):**

1. is going to die — the evidence is in front of you
2. will take / I'll take — decided at the moment of speaking
3. are going to plug in — decided on Sunday and written on the list
4. will come back — an opinion, with *I think*
5. is going to submit — planned for a week

**3.6 B (future forms):** 1. is going to rebuild · 2. Are … going to download (or Will … download) · 3. are not going to get · 4. will go / is going to go · 5. will not move

**3.6 C (present perfect or past simple):** 1. failed · 2. have not missed · 3. queued · 4. has written

**Mini-quiz:** 1. it'll · 2. will · 3. *gonna* · 4. upload · 5. in use · 6. inverter · 7. priority · 8. *She submitted it on Thursday* — Thursday is a finished time, and the present perfect cannot share a sentence with one · 9–12. teacher judgement

### Teacher Notes {: #teacher-notes }

**What changed from Lesson 5, and what deliberately did not.** The passage is 504 words against Lesson 5's 481, and that is the point: **the length stops climbing here.** Lessons 1 to 5 went 185, 244, 320, 400, 481 — about a quarter longer every week, which is faster than anybody consolidates. Lessons 6, 7 and 8 all sit at about 500. Difficulty still rises, but through the grammar step, the density of the vocabulary, and how much of the text is argument rather than story. The question set is untouched: ten questions, the same eight types, in the same order. She should recognise every question on sight and spend all of her attention on the text.

**The one real difficulty.** Not the forms — *will* and *going to* are both easy to build — but choosing between them. Arabic marks the future with one particle and does not split it this way, so the instinct is to use whichever came first in the textbook. The rule that actually works is in 3.4: **the list is *going to*; the conversation is *will*.** If the decision existed before the sentence began, it is *going to*. If it was made inside the sentence, or is only an opinion, it is *will*. Make her say *why* in 3.6 A: the reason matters more than the answer.

**Why the pronunciation part is the one to protect.** A student can write *will* perfectly and never once hear it, because in speech it is a single consonant hung on the end of the pronoun — *it'll*, *she'll*, *we'll*. The same student hears *gonna* and connects it to nothing she has been taught. Part 05 says it plainly: **write *going to*, say /ˈɡənə/.** The trap in its third section is worth two extra minutes — *I'm going to the college* keeps the full sound, because there *going* is a real verb of movement.

**On the "Come back to" section.** It takes the present perfect from Lesson 4 and adds the rule held back the first time: it cannot share a sentence with a finished time. *I have finished it yesterday* is among the most common errors at this level, and it survives for years if nobody names it. The test is mechanical — is the time expression closed? — so she can apply it without thinking once she has seen it once.

**Why this story.** Five passages have followed one person. This one follows a group, which is what the future tenses need: plans are made by people talking to each other, and *will* only makes sense when somebody is in the room to decide something in front of you. It also lets the passage be concrete about things she already knows — an inverter, a schedule that changes every month, a queue of downloads — without being *about* them. They are competent people with a method, which is both true and exactly what the grammar requires.

**Success criteria for Lesson 6.** The student should be able to:

- answer L1–L4 correctly on the second hearing;
- hear *it'll be ready* and *we're gonna start* and write both out in full;
- choose between *will* and *going to*, and say why;
- form the negative and the question of both;
- avoid the present perfect with *yesterday*, *last Tuesday*, *at six o'clock*;
- use 10 of the 14 key words in her own sentence;
- write 14 sentences of plan with fewer than 4 future errors.

**If it is too easy:** keep the length where it is and raise the density instead — ask for the writing task in 18 sentences, with three *will* / *going to* choices justified in the margin.
**If it is too hard:** drop part 05 to recognition only — hear it, do not produce it — and drill 3.4 alone for a second week. Length will not be the problem this time, which is the reason for holding it flat.

**A note on spaced recall.** `03-vocabulary.mp3` ends with five Lesson 4 words — *connection, website, account, password, update*. Lesson 5 recalled Lesson 3, so the two-lesson gap holds. Lesson 5's words are due back in Lesson 7.

**A note on the games.** This is the first lesson with **five** instead of two: the crossword and the word search as before, plus memory pairs, a criss-cross clued in Arabic, and a cryptogram. All five are generated from the same vocabulary block, so none of them can drill a word the lesson does not teach. The memory game has three settings — icons, meanings, mixed — and its drawings live in `icons.json` at the repository root, shared by every lesson. Lessons 1 to 5 still have two games each; giving them the other three needs drawings for about seventy more words, and that is a separate decision.

segments.say: Slow version. The passage, read slowly, one time.

There are four of them, and between them they have one inverter, one battery, two laptops and a list. The list is on the back of a door in a room at the college, and every Sunday evening they write next week's plan on it. The plan is not about the work. The plan is about the power. Everything else on the list follows from that.

The electricity in their part of the city comes in two blocks, and the schedule changes every month. This month it is on from six in the morning until nine, and again from seven at night until eleven. Seven hours. Dalia, who keeps the list, says the first thing you learn is that seven hours is enough, if you decide what each hour is for before it starts.

So the list has two columns. On the left is what they are going to do while the power is on: plug in both laptops, charge the battery, download the week's lecture videos, and send the group project up to the cloud. On the right is what they will do when it goes off: read, write, plan, and argue about the design. Every line has a name beside it, so nobody is waiting for somebody else to begin.

Yousef is in charge of the downloads. "I am going to start the big files at six," he said on Sunday, "and I'll leave the small ones until the end. If the bandwidth is bad, we will still have the lectures." He has learned not to queue everything at once. Last month he put eleven files in the queue at six o'clock and had four of them by nine.

Nour is going to finish the database work before Thursday, because the deadline is Thursday night and she is going to submit it on time this week. Hani is going to rebuild the spare laptop, the one with the broken socket, and he says it will be ready by Wednesday. Nobody believes him. He says that every week.

There are rules on the list as well, and all of them are about priority. The battery is for the router first and the laptops second. Nothing that can be done on paper is done on a screen while the power is on. And whatever else happens, the project goes to the cloud before eleven, because a file that exists in one place does not really exist.

Dalia will not say that the plan always works. Last Tuesday the generator in the building below them failed at half past seven, and the two blocks became one. They lost three hours. But they had sent the project up at seven, so they lost three hours of work and nothing else, which is the whole reason for the rule.

On Sunday she will write the next list, and it will look much like this one. "We are not going to get more hours," she says. "So we are going to get better at the hours we have."
